revisions.title: The search returns to aporia
revisions.body: The search for the kingly art does not arrive at a usable definition. Socrates reports that he and the young man have fallen into aporia about the knowledge that would make them happy, and Crito names the impasse as great. Hear the scene as a return to the question, not a completed result.

revisions.title: The dog becomes a father
revisions.body: The dog becomes Ctesippus’s father through a shift in relation. The dog belongs to Ctesippus, and the dog has fathered puppies; the argument then treats ownership as though it were kinship. Its force comes from sliding between two meanings of belonging, not from establishing a genuine family relation.

revisions.title: When a qualified good becomes unlimited
revisions.body: The sophistic move is to turn a qualified good into an unlimited quantity. Ctesippus grants that medicine is useful when needed; Euthydemus then asks whether that means taking as much as possible, even a wagonload of hellebore. The pressure lies in removing the condition, not in discovering a medical rule.

revisions.title: When the craft changes its patient
revisions.body: Dionysodorus quietly changes who the craft acts on. Socrates grants that a butcher cuts and skins; the sophist then treats the butcher as the thing cut and skinned, so butchering the butcher becomes “fitting.” The same grammatical slide is repeated with the bronzeworker and potter.

revisions.title: Judge philosophy, not its practitioners
revisions.body: Crito’s unease concerns the people who claim to educate, but Socrates shifts the test to philosophy itself. Every pursuit has many poor practitioners and few serious ones, so bad examples do not settle the practice. Examine philosophy directly; if it proves worthy, pursue and practice it with the children.

body: "At 300e–301a, the exchange shifts the meaning of “present” without announcing the shift. Socrates begins with beautiful things that possess some beauty; Dionysodorus answers as though being present made one thing identical with the other—an ox turns Socrates into an ox, and Dionysodorus into Dionysodorus. One way to hear the move is as a test of predicate scope: a relation is made to do the work of an identity. Socrates then praises the brothers as craftsmen, and the craft examples drive that confidence toward absurd conclusions at 301d–301e. Track what each predicate is being asked to do, not merely whether the replies sound grammatical."
